How do I start trading/investing if I only have $1000? A full guide

So, we're running both a 10k -> 100k trading challenge and a 200k -> 1 mil "investing" challenge all publicly on twitter and they are going well so far and we're making money.

But one question or comment I do often get asked is "well that's cool but what if I don't have 10k, or 200k, Astro?". Or more general: "How much do I need to get started with investing?". Or just people getting discouraged with: "well good for you that you're winning on all those positions, but I don't have that type of money and am not making nearly as much let alone making a living".

Firstly just wanted to address here to not let that demotivate you. But because the answer to those questions is slightly more nuanced, I'll get into those grey areas right here with this post because it would be unfair to just say "just start investing now and you will make it in 10 years".

Because it does depend to some extent to your strategy, incomes, capital available, where you come from. But regardless, it's a skill worth learning and if you want to make it, a skill you'll have to face mastering regardless of how much money you have, so why not start now? If you get good, things move quick. I'll show you how.

Skill is more important than capital

So, you all probably understand that trade-vesting is scalable, just like any business. I use trade-vesting here, a term for trading + investing that exist because doing both properly is essentially the same, investing is trading on a monthly/quarterly timeframe and yes most investors do sell assets too, ignore Michael Saylor here for a second.

Scalable means that your wealth general growths (or decreases if you're still learning) exponentially. I've shown that on the screenshot below.

And that's powerful, but also deceitful at the same time. It's powerful because regardless how much you have, 10x'ing is always practically the same, but the opposite (0.1x'ing) is also easy if you're not careful. That's why trading and investing is crucial to master, because if you don't and you have a lot of money from your day job, it's very easy to turn it into little money instead of more. So through scaling, climbing the ladder is much easier, as well as descending.

That's why getting through "the learners phase" (which we all have to) is critical to start doing as early as possible and also for as little cost/mistakes as possible. It would be disingenuous to tell you I didn't have my fair share of losses during my learners phase. It's not a joke when someone (me) tells you to "focus on the skill of making money over the money itself".

So with that said, don't worry for example if you turn 5k into 500 if that teaches you a valuable lesson. Those lessons are extremely valuable and don't even require any bit of journaling. "Your losses are your best journal".

What if you mastered the skill?

So that's the first point answered. It doesn't matter how much you have if you're in the learners phase. You just want to put your blood on the line, try to turn it into more, and stimulate the positive feedback loop and make money if you succeed. And stimulate the negative feedback loop and lose money when you lose. 

Okay but what if you're a skilled trade-vestor? What if you're past the learners phase? Well now the power of exponential returns is on your side. So let's say you 10x every 3 years after tax (I think that's very realistic), then whether you start with 1k or 10k to end up with ten million is just 12 or 15 years away, which is only a difference of three years. And that's why, yet again, it doesn't matter what you have, because trade-vesting is scalable.

And that shows why, as long as you have the skill of this craft, you're golden regardless, even if you have "nothing" and even if you lose everything sometime down the line, even twice (I know a couple).

What if I am broke?

Now I can hear you, "what if I literally have 1$, I want to turn it into 10 mil, that still takes me 21 years (assuming the same rate of 10x every 3 years).

Yes, I hear you. "Don't neglect your 9-to-5" is my answer. Because like I said, there is indeed nuance to this answer. And that's why I drew the graph below.

In short, the graph tells you that if you have a 9-5, it makes more sense to work for one hour instead of 3 years to turn your first dollar into 10$, and with dedication, it's very doable to save 10k or even more in a year or two. But the more you have, the less it makes sense to have a 9-to-5 until it makes 0 sense.

9-to-5 versus trade-vesting

I drew out a typical curve of what saving from a 9-to-5 could look like, versus the curve of a trade-vestor. Keep in mind that this chart is a logarithmic scale, so the 9-to-5'ers savings over time flatten out. The trade-vestor's curve should be linear. But because at the beginning, you're learning and focused on improving skill and mind (mindset/mentality), it starts slow and ultimately steepens. And once you're a master investor, it goes typically linear. 

Now you also see I drew it as flattening out afterwards. That's just for correctness, because as capital scales, liquidity becomes an issue. And to remain optimal your strategies require some change because multiplying millions of dollars isn't the same as thousands. So even returns of trade-vesting flatten out on the log scale. But don't worry, once that happens, you already made it by a long shot.

And I do understand it's a different story in a second or third world country in terms of saving money, but the principles still apply, the optimum to transition from more 9-to-5 towards trade-vesting just has to start with less capital, but the threshold of having made it in your country is lower at the same time. So everyone dedicated enough, can win up to the point of "making it" with a more or less even playing field regardless of your background. Explains why you see stories of people from a poor background make it.

Conclusion

Hope this posts gives some insight of "how much you need to invest". Not that much, really, perhaps a few months/a year of saving and time goes fast. But the most important point here is to start learning (or improving) it today because that will stick for a lifetime and the sooner you master it, the sooner exponential returns take over and can quit your 9-to-5, because the skill is a requirement.

"Focus on the skill of making money rather than making money itself", is not a joke or a meme, whenever someone (me) mentions that.

With that said I hope you are encouraged to keep learning and applying, to climb up that ladder and not slide down instead.

Quoting this because I can see this being the burning question.

So I just called the $BTC.D top (and the start of the 4 yearly alt season), does that mean a $BTC top?

Short answer: no, it does not.

I still think $BTC can and will go up further, above and beyond 100k. A $BTC.D top is not the same as a $BTC top.

Remember that last cycle, $BTC.D topped in the first week of December 2020 when $BTC was at 20k. But $BTC topped only in April 2021 when it was at 65k. So even though alt season technically started since the $BTC.D top, $BTC still pulled a 3x afterwards, but alts pulled far larger moves during that same period, whereas before, they barely moved and the majority underperformed compared to $BTC.

So yes, $BTC can still go up. But the overall "feel" of the crypto market will be a lot different.

It could look like a few months of both altcoin holders and $BTC holders winning at the same time (but altcoins printing a lot harder anyways just by the nature of their thin liquidity), followed by $BTC holders not really winning anymore, because only altcoins holders are winning now. And then, once $BTC.D is very low again, we expect the market to transition into a top.

Also a friendly reminder that this is a high timeframe call (happening once every four years). A macro $BTC.D top doesn't mean a massive macro drop immediately. That's not how that happens ever.

Big money (located on the high timeframes) takes time to move especially , just think of moving a large weight. That's why the markets constantly move from big expansion, to range, to compression, to expansion again, gradually and constantly shifting between slowed and accelerated fashion, just like a pendulum.

So with the $BTC altcoin rotation, the same applies, just like any move, this transition will be gradual. The top is in I think, which usually happens during the transitionary stage. So yes, we still can see days where $BTC dominates, but the overall momentum has shifted, just now, IMO.

So let's stay off the cool aid, keep it level headed, but at the same time very well acknowledge the conditions we are in. 
 
We're going to see change and you're not going to want to fade that.

Regarding Stoplosses + guide on trading "without a stoploss"

So 5 days ago, we started a 10k -> 100k altcoin trading challenge where we show every single move for free on twitter for the world to copy.

It's been received very well (we're up 10% already despite missing some large moves by a hair) and the ones who followed have been making lots of money and at the same time actionably identifying ahead of everyone else and understanding how to trade these types of conditions. Teaching you how not to FOMO, but also not to miss out on essential moves by picking the right levels, timing and pair it with deep research of how I expect these conditions to evolve.

Easily the single most asked question is "why are you not using a stoploss".

It's a very common one because the standard of retail trading is to put a hard SL at a certain level, which the market makers can spot and run before they hit your profit levels.

Just kidding of course. But at least, "putting a hard SL is a must" is what the majority of trading gurus teach you because they all learnt trading from each other or like to echo chamber or just haven't considered an open mind to different options in an out of the box way. I'm not saying that is wrong. I use them myself.

But I come from quite a different background and besides that classical style of trading mentioned above, I also have some years in institutional trading which is indeed, mostly without a "stoploss".

See large hedge funds for instance don't have the ability to just close a position at a precise level at market (which is what a hard SL is). That would cause immense slippage. Instead they get out manually, upon invalidation of a certain market move on higher timeframes, which is also what we do. So, we still use an SL on this challenge, just not a hard SL.

"Okay so you use a manual SL, cool Astro, I get it but what if the market drops 80% overnight in a single H12 candle and we were long."

First of all, that's very unlikely to happen and only happened a few times in history across all crypto markets in the top 100. Only rug pulls have shown this behavior in the past.

Secondly, we don't go all in on one project (for the small chances it rug pulls or something), we'd still be fine even if that happens.

Thirdly, the only reason to use an SL is to take you out of the market in case it drops overnight and you are asleep. Otherwise, you can set alerts, see them as you're awake and get out manually. And because H12 candles are never bigger than 20% moves from open to close (back test this), and also because our leverage is never larger than 3x total, the chances of liquidation overnight are smaller than getting struck by lightning, which would kill you anyway.

And lastly, this is after all a limits only challenge, so setting an SL by default is an at market order. Reason for the limits only choice is because that is by far the easiest way to follow without missing out because you were not online. It also prevents large pools of liquidity (the SL I show) for the market makers to grab.

So with all of that, I hope you now both understand that trading without an SL is as low of a risk if not lower than exposing yourself to the market makers with a big flag showing where your forced losses are, as long as you know what you are doing, keep leverage low, and position accordingly. 

So instead of showing the market makers where they make us lose, I'm showcasing you the proper way of what it's like to be the market maker ourselves.

If you are still scared for a rug pull/overnight liquidation (this is crypto after all), I recommend putting a hard SL 30% down from original entry yourself, just to prevent that loss. Since our positions are smaller than half of size of the full account, that would only result in a 15% loss in the worst case of that low chance happening, as our picks are all focused on top 300 altcoins.

So accounting for all of that, I think this challenge is a nice refreshing change, to show you what's possible and that not every trade requires a hard SL, manual trading is possible even if you sleep 8 hours a day, and, it's working, isn't it?

Why I love market cycle theory - Part 2

So about 2 months ago, I've written an extensive part 1 on why I believe market cycles work so well, how to identify them and last but not least, not underestimate their power and effect especially in crypto but pretty much in every single market.

And the 15th of September wasn't a randomly picked time to make that post. It was just days after $BTC planted the major higher low at 53k in our opinion at the time, a low where we said, with at the time high conviction "this is very likely the last time $BTC visits low 50's, next time we go up and break out".

And here we are, nearly double prices today, at the time, I would say, something the world would not have ever believed so soon.

There was fear of recession, Warren buffet selling, OI at ATH's, Michael Bury going massively short, and the fud cutting rates (which typically means downside).

That's why I said, "market cycles are overarching and in control of markets and all of the above (such as monetary policy), so both respect cyclical theory and cyclical theory is leading both price and the factors mentioned above".

And I just wanted to mention another mechanism of why the 4 year cycle particularly works so well and it's quite simple:

For some reason, 4 years is the time it takes for people to completely forget what the same exact conditions were like exactly 4 years ago. Whether that was:

"What it felt like $BTC planting a bottom at 3k, and 4 years later at 15k". 
"What it felt like $BTC.D surging hard and $BTC pumping yet alts not doing anything"
"What it felt like for $ETH to not do anything and being called dead"
"And what it will feel like to 

It feels like 4 years is a good time to get fully attached to a narrative and expecting that to never change ever again. And if you have any friend groups in crypto (or just spend time on social media), you can see it. It's crystal clear and obvious.

"Memes have taken over"
"$BTC season will never end this time"
"$BTC will never stop ranging"
"This time is different than 4 years ago, whatever it may be"

Believe it or not but there also was a time (called Q1, Q2 2021) where alts were believed to be the new thing and $BTC was never going to take over a 50% market share ever again, never going back above 50% dominance because "the world adopted crypto and there are so many useful altcoins". And now, all those exact same altcoins are now called useless, meme, "speculation". Fascinating, isn't it. Those who were around, will understand what I mean.

In crypto, if something doesn't go down, but doesn't go up while the rest is: it's very likely cued for rotation (on all timeframes).

But, if something trends down over time while the others keep going up, more than two rotations on the lower timeframes in succession, then there's substance to worry.

To give an example: let's say there are three categories: memes, dino's and $ETH. And let's say the rotation expected in the cycle is: 1⃣ memes => 2⃣ dino's => 3⃣ $ETH. (not saying it is, just an example)

Well because cycles are fractal and intertwined, it should show on the lower timeframes too. So you should receive early warnings of the 1⃣ memes => 2⃣ $ETH => 3⃣ dino's. rotation not happening.

So if there would be 4 days where: 1⃣ Day 1: memes up => 2⃣ Day 2: dino's up=> 3⃣ Day 3: memes up => 4⃣ Day 4: dino's up again (and $ETH is missed out of the rotation twice), then there's substance for concern that $ETH may also not run for the cycle.

So the key here really is to see that $ETH did have extreme green days and it shows because it's still up nicely from ~$900, its cycle low. So it hasn't been forgotten out of rotation and is just holding a range because it's lagging compared to all the rest in the larger timeframe cyclical rotation.

And with that said, I'm putting my money where my talk is, and I sold the rest of my $SOL for $ETH here, just now, for a few reasons.

Why $SOLETH has topped, the analysis

Very strong reasons in fact, due to some simple, yet powerful high timeframe asset rotation analysis. Asset rotations are not a new thing and not "crypto only". They exist in every market and used to be very prominent in the early days of commodity trading (and still are).

In crypto, they work even better because there still is so much unaware and fresh capital present, new to investing in high volatility terrain, easy to take advantage of, especially in altcoins. And whales love to take advantage of that.

The way it works is simple. Every time a large (top 10) asset breaks its old all time high, its highest competitor often gets rotated towards and thus receives relative strength.

Why? Because that's when it hits news lines, that's when everyone on the sidelines starts buying, and the whales start rotating into other assets, you already know these things.

But what's more important is that this is all backed very strongly by data, still to this day. And there is nowhere near enough talk about these types of trend shifts and capital rotations, instead everyone just keeps on bull posting $SOL and holding $SOL memes on chain. Another reason why I'm writing this post.

So regarding the data, let's check the simplest and oldest capital rotation: $BTC to $ETH.

When does capital rotate from $BTC to $ETH? When $BTC breaks ATH.

Below I drew the line every time $BTC broke ATH on the $BTCETH chart. Keep in mind this is the $BTCETH chart not the $ETHBTC chart.

So over the entire history, that already gives three significant data points.

But there is more. Second chart shows the rotation behavior between $ETH and $ETC, another strong beta play, and so also another strong data point showing that whenever $ETH broke ATH, $ETC gains relative strength.

Third one: $ADA and $ETH. Especially in the early days, $ADA was known/put forward to be the prime $ETH killer (so much for that). As a beta play on $ETH, the chart shows that when $ETH broke old ATH the $ETHADA chart put in a top for the cycle.

On $ETHADA, you do see one thing: $ETH hasn't broken ATH yet, but $ADA already seemed to have started its run. That doesn't mean that is a bad data point. All it means is that $ETH putting in an ATH for a high probability $ADA beta play isn't a requirement. But IF it happens, it is a strong reversal signal.

So since $SOL indeed broke ATH and $ETH is the clear $SOL beta this cycle, this leads to the conclusion that $SOLETH likely has topped, the moment it happened.

An important trait of a successful trader/investor

What makes an okay trader/investor into a great one is someone who respects time, waits for a certain time, then deeply analyses what the market looks like at that time, verifies if the current price could be a major top or bottom, and acts accordingly with conviction.

"Don't try to predict the markets, react to the markets".

And that quote, doesn't mean to buy or sell way late, it means reacting to the markets at exact (or very close to) reversals/points of pivot/change in conditions.

This mentality beats "waiting for a certain price point or level stubbornly" any time of the day, putting ego in the way and thinking "you are right".

It is possible to know where price goes in high timeframe discovery but it is much easier and more accurate to "wait it out whilst making money" and then detect when a shifts in direction (range <=> uptrend <=> downtrend) is likely to occur, as long as you put the time and effort in.

Reason people don't like this approach is because it doesn't tell you by what time you will retire and most people trade their P&L, not the markets.

Whilst successful traders/investors simply look to consistently make money without ego or being stubborn.

There is a 0% chance the crypto market topped.

So, in conjunction with our crypto trading, "bull run final phase" masterplan which started with calling the 55k bottom (see the quoted tweet for the start of the series of calls), the 63k breakout pivot and subsequently, altcoin season, we researched the optimal times to launch both the 200k -> 1 mil spot altcoin trading challenge and the 10k -> 100k altcoin trading challenge and allocated ourselves massively long and into spot right after the 55k bottom, before the ATH breakout, during, and even after into coins that haven't run much yet.

So that's a lot of capital we've been having at risk on the long side. Not only myself, but the entire community has been printing along as I have been openly and publicly making these calls on twitter with full transparency. And yes, most of those positions are comfortable now and up a lot, but it's equally important to know when to stop, change bias, or implement changes or approach to both challenges and all our positions. Because yes I have set target goals (1 mil and 100k respectively for the challenge), but that doesn't mean they can be reached going long only, and the key is to listen to the market, not your P&L.

"Trade the market, not your P&L".

So it's important to stay sharp and always look when and where the top will be.

For that, I have exactly 7 of my most reliable metrics in place, and will be revealing them over time.

And, funding rate is not one of them either as it is not something I clamp towards, because high across-the-board funding rates are not a guarantee for a market top, as the market "can keep going for a while" and you may miss out on the biggest portions of the gains if you use that metric only for a top. Besides, I never recommend using only one metric, despite what you typically see on twitter. You know we do it different and like to perform in depth analysis, and that is why I have 7 in place.

So funding rates are not a top signal, but consider this a warm-up to spark awareness, to not drink any cool-aid, and to stick to our core strategy of always staying ahead of the herd and go against the herd when applicable. Which is exactly how we were able to call the upside since September in the first place.

So, how to use funding rates to call the top?

I didn't, and, like I said, you can't IMO. But what they do tell you, is when the market has not topped. And because calling a top is binary (it's in or it's not), that is almost as useful as calling a top.

So again, funding rates do not guarantee a top, but they are historically, a requirement for a market top. I.e., the crypto market has never topped without at least a total perps trading volume weighted average funding rate of 70% APR of the top 20 coins. And because that weighted average APR currently is around 18.9%, this means that,

historically, based on every single significant market top in history since the mass adoption of altcoins i.e.:

The 2018 top in January,
The 2019 top in June,
The 2021 top in May,
The 2021 Top in November
The 2024 Top in March,

there is a 0% chance that the market has topped.

So, whenever I see a bear post right now of sometimes even "experienced" traders/investors, or someone dropping the good old "be careful" (someone please explain to me how to "be careful" in markets...), I firstly respect them taking their time to write it, secondly, look critically at what they have to say, and thirdly, probably will be fading it because it is most likely data presented with a large selectivity bias especially if posted today.

So with that said, I hope this gives both clarity of my current outlook on the markets, as well as a tiny look into how I approach things to stay as accurate as I can at all times.

That's also in alignment with our $BTC plan which could very well drag this out into mid January.

So how to position spot?

A typical way is using half to buy at a very good point in time (like now), and the other half to buy/ad significantly lower and significantly later in time (both are important) "the late low compound buy", or if the market recovers earlier and shows confirmation to the upside instead an equal time period later "the late higher compound buy". Both are good and subjected to "taking whatever the market gives".

I am doing a similar strategy here but over the years I learnt to split it into three instead. That makes it more forgiving and at the same time, gives us probably both the late lower compound buy and a final buy at confirmation, especially when starting early and when you are certain there is likely another sweep of the lows or extended periods of ranging or the dump has fully settled yet.

Cycle theory, a tax payer perspective

You know I am a big advocate of market cycle theory. We used cycle theory to both predict the 2023 $BTC and $SOL bottom with conviction, the large leg pre and post ETF, and to position for the last bottom we would see before the massive breakout, timed and hinted per quoted tweet on the second of September. In the tweet we reminded extensively how important cycle theory is and to not fear black swans or news events. I wrote at the time, to not fear the War in Middle East, which was, indeed "the emotional reason" why price wasn't moving. News of world war 3 which is long forgotten now, but at the time, best believe how dominating it was and supposedly more important than cycle theory. 

And that isn't the only time. It seems as if cycle theory receives unrightful objection before each and every big move, proving everyone wrong, reactivating memories, when it's too late, "the narrative lag".

It's a shame as I have been using cycle theory firmly my entire career pretty much, starting with commodities, but even more prominent in crypto, extracting money from markets using it for 8+ years now. Probably a reason why the word cycles has been part of my twitter bio ever since I decided to start posting.

But why do I like cycles the most? Because they get uneducated people or disbelievers each and every time as the near term memory loss fallacy and the momentum mindset "trade strength, trade the trend" (on any market) always happens to go exactly against cyclical reversals at peak complacency stages. So even if people are aware, peak complacency overwhelms the decisions of a trader/investor at exactly those large reversals.

Take the 15.5k bottom of $BTC for example, how many people expected 12k and therefore ignored the fact that it was time to buy regardless of price even if they knew it was time? Same at the Nov 2021 market peak (how many expected 100k+ "why else would we go back to high 60's"). Same with the recent 44k calls ("Middle eastern war, WW3"), same with the recent $BTC.D peak "$BTC will dominate for the rest of time, institutions are in", same with the $ETHBTC bottom "$ETH is worthless, $ETH foundation is selling" or $SOLETH peak "SOL is the new $ETH". "Memes are the new paradigm, dino's will never go up ever again".

So clearly, they are both useful and effective.

I'm looking to write a detailed post on how cycles work work and how the stages transition for the ones that do choose to believe in it and get a full understanding as especially in crypto, the transition of stages are crystal clear and typically allow for rather early confirmation.

But for the other ones who don't like to believe in something "random" (I hear you), another, hands-on way to look at why they make sense to work and why there is no way around it, is to simply look at taxes. Taxes, yes. One of the most important elements of trading/investing/businesses.

Rich people pay way more taxes (both in absolute value and proportionally) than less wealthy people.

So if a smart whale buys in (as an investment) say before the start of this leg somewhere (June 2024), then I can assure you he wants to pay long term capital gains taxes and avoid short term capital gains taxes. In most countries, that means holding longer than 1 year.

So, if smart money wants to buy low and sell high, then the time difference between low and high prices is at least 1 year long. So a bull market including accumulation and distribution stages, can not last less than 1 year by the sheer nature of how most financial systems work on a national level. So that means, there is a fixed time how long bull (and bear markets) last, and it's usually a stretched out period of time. And fixed intervals, means predictable interval, which means cycles.

Going deeper, taxes are charged annually. And why is that? Where does "the annum" stem from? It's one year, one planetary rotation of the earth around the sun.

So whether you want it or not. Cycles are everywhere, purely by us being part of planet earth and how a large part of our financial system is based on that.

Just makes me think it's kind of a radical decision to just ignore such facts, especially if your own finances are at stake.

So, after the 30% overnight drop we received and with all the necessary management moves post drop made, including a de risk on two large positions at the top of the bounce, alongside scoring a short on $ADA, what I typically do is a thorough reassessment.

Because, we were clearly planning for a larger drop, a longer period of ranging and decided to TP more aggressively. And yet still, the account reduced from 20k to about 15k post dump overnight, which is  <yes> manageable, but slightly too big of a drop, I think it's only fair to admit that the downside could have been limited on my part.

And I think it's also only fair to admit I clearly made some slight management error recently aside from doing all the rest right. In total, we're still up 57% as of currently. But the damage could have been limited somewhat more.

I am here to help you through the reality of trading, so I'm here fully sharing my thoughts on how to progress every step along the way, because we're going for 100k, through all ups and downs, so that includes every necessary step.

This is a marathon, an emotionless marathon that is, so there is no quitting mid way through.

And you're free to jump in on the bandwagon at any point in time because I have been fully sharing everything with full transparency so you can immediately see what is going on and with some logic, how to join in (always feel free to ask how to join in).

So with that, here goes the re-assessment.

The good

On the upside, we are still around 15.8k on the account, we had a large drop, and the high timeframes still look completely fine. The market makers and whales also have a mechanism in place to range the markets after a large move. They do this because, if they want to drop the market, that is their way of exiting their longs from lower, whilst being hedged with shorts as they continue to reaccumulate or distribute.

We indeed had a large move up on every single altcoin,  so now the logical expectations are for a range to form. That means that both range high and low get retested multiple times, allowing us to de risk higher.

Furthermore, it is still Monday, the first move is likely an opposite move of the overall weekly move, so that also supports the range idea.

At the same time, the $BTC.D top is still fully valid, so this type of drop is still within the general trend of "alt season."

Finally, there is also a chance that $BTC again solo rallies hard, whilst alts stay sideways, and that altcoins fully catch up after $BTC is done. This final scenario is the most bullish and would help us to get straight back into making money fast.

So, that's quite a list of good news. Would be a shame to ignore all those key factors, miss out, or let emotions get the better of you by closing everything here, or abandon the challenge, or be stubborn now and exit later on more retests of range lows.

The bad

The bad are the mistakes made. Clearly, I was slightly too eager on bidding POI zones that were too close.

They were all valid, but as a higher timeframe range forms, the most aggressive bid zones don't work anymore.

Combined with an "unlucky" 30% big overnight drop, and holding positions through, that causes a 25% drop in account after the local bounce (right now).

$METIS also barely front ran quite a large TP which also ended up hurting upon the drop as that was one of the biggest positions in the red.

So to correct that, I would simply lower size on earlier bids, and ad heavier on later bids and overall reduce leverage as each weekly leg grows, because we do have the luxury to do that since our strength is to get aggressive early as we have been doing, and which is the main reason the account is still up strong. If all is done correctly, account would have been closer to 20k if not higher. Things to remember next time.

Apart from that, not much to do, other than just managing your way through the range and slowly de risking at optimal points, as the market always allows you to do so.

If it doesn't even do that and just go straight down from here (highly unlikely but "what if"), then I am simply out once we hit 8k as a balance and take the 2k losses total on the account, live in the trenches for longer and go back because then the altcoin bear market truly is back.

Can happen, but don't see it likely.

This is a high risk challenge despite "playing it safe" after all. And we're still up 60% in 5 weeks which is still way faster than hitting the planned 10x through limits only in a year time.

The plan

So now, the plan. 

The main plan is to "de risk as unscathed as possible" whilst making money through trading the range for a while (like we just did with the $ADA short). That overall plan allows us to still grow the account, whilst at the same time limiting losses.

We know there is a high chance that we range now (almost guaranteed). That means that midrange at the very least, and sometimes range high (or a lower high) gets reached.

I could draw this out on all positions, but in summary, just use $TOTAL3.

If 0.5 of this dump gets reached on $TOTAL3 (or on most positions we still have open), then thanks to bids we had filled (below that 0.5 level), the balance will still end up at about 19k, indeed pretty much unscathed.

From there, I look to exit positions and sit on the sidelines to see if the market performs the bearish retest and rejects or if $BTC does a solo break out, easy longs as alts lag on $BTC.

So the problem is not "if we are getting a range with higher retests". The problem is rather about getting too greedy when price moves into retest territory and you don't get out and how you're managing that range.

I indeed will manage as optimally as humanly possible, and if $BTC decides to break out and run aggressively, leaving altcoins sideways for somewhat longer, then it's simply time to buy again for a ride, continuing to ride up with the 18k balance, multiplying it further. If bearish retests happen, might look for shorts, wait out for a pattern to form, or at least allow some time to range, before further clarity.

Full plan and thoughts are also drawn out on the chart below, easy to follow.

Conclusion

So, despite some errors, still doing "fine". Account is still up well above where we started, well ahead of schedule and even more so if this range plan plays out, I am not complaining.

But at the same time, there were some mistakes management wise which cost us more than needed. I won't be the one to hide that. This is a fully transparent challenge. Simply going to continue with managing our way through that.

Why confluence is important and how to navigate the statistical nature of markets

Whenever I post a full trading plan on where I think price is going (up, down, or sideways - yes, there are three "directions" to price), I receive several reoccurring types of comments such as "nice plan on thinking we go up, but there is a CME gap below", or "nice plan on thinking we go up, but the spot premium on obscure exchange X is negative"

Firstly, I appreciate your comments, and I value them especially if they are things I look for myself. But then I even get comments like "your posts are so long, can't you just tell us in one sentence what you think price will do?".

And then it's obvious you likely put too much weight on one simple fact. As the length of my posts has to do with that fact that I look for confluence, strong confluence that is, the most important confluence. That's what shapes a trade idea and confidence. It is indeed hard to express all relevant (and only relevant!) confluences in one single line to form my trading plan.

Yes, one single piece of edge could save you, and it could even play out, against all odds and against the trader/investor (me) who shapes his plan based on a full array of confluences, and that trader then may think he's a genius temporarily.

But experienced traders/Investors know that confluences beat one single piece of edge over time, and that beginners luck can be detrimental in that sense.

"Wait until the cards break even" as we say.

So yes, your CME gap fill or Okex spot vs Binance Futures spot discount might play out, and if you're right, against my range of confluences, I'll always give you credit, but it's up to you to realize if you're subjected to out-of-confluence luck because only you know your full historic trading record.

All fairness to you, because whether you are right or wrong in a statistically driven world is one of the most challenging aspects for developing traders/investors.

You could be doing something right and lose money, or wrong and make money. Our brain isn't wired to reward the above and you spiral down. Only way to break that spiral is to tell yourself "I don't care about making or losing money, I just take the right actions and know I will make money in the long run".

And one of those right actions are IMO looking for confluences instead of laziness and crutching to just one trick you may have in the markets.

And the more confluences you get, the more knowledgeable and experienced you become, the less you will have the statistical issue (you will win more). But while developing, you have neither, so it's a tough barrier to overcome, as if all things are set up against you until it all starts to turn around and turn around fast.

Even if you have one piece of amazing edge, with a 100% accuracy, over a sample size of 20 or more, it could still not work out (what if it stops working, I've been there).

So yes, confluences are important. They give robustness to your system, they exponentially increase the odds of an idea going to your favor and they allow a margin of error and lead the decision to you, tell you both where the market goes, and how clear your read is (aligned confluences, or combatting). And depending on the type (directional confluence, or magnet + level confluence), you can get a great idea where the market is going on all timeframes.

Look for confluences. And don't crutch on one moving average, one gap, or one seemingly obvious trend. You may call a genius move short term, but it will hurt you long term.

Trading is boring. It's analysing all confluences and taking the smartest decision and make (a lot of) money, compounding over time, sometimes less, sometimes massive amounts. But it's going mayhem and calling a wild move, making it in one trade, etc.

It can work to some extent, but we all know how it likely ends.

Let's not beat around the bush.

Clearly a +CRT if and only if if the current candle closes above the previous candles' low. 

And the specific beauty of this chart is, that you can easily see it will close above, even in advance, so you can prepare and be ready to execute (preparation kills hesitation)

How do I know?

Here simply because of the long wick to the upside on this current candle. Which can only happen upon a low timeframe upside true upside displacement after the candle open (ICT time and price). Extra bonus is three candles down at least, which also gives a high probability of a full CRT reversal.

And since it happens during  CRT candle #️2, its paired with a turtle soup, with large displacement.

Which also means that any light and weak sweeps are false, and you only want to long clear and strong TS + judas swings (as CRT should be and as they mostly are).

So, a simple chart, but with a lot of hidden clues, and those hidden clues are key (for me at least) to execute properly.

Because "an analysis/setup without execution is useless".

Speaking of execution, I've drawn it out in red on the chart.

I usually enter on CRT candle #️3, but with a long wick (displacement) on candle #️2 (ICT time and price), it's IMO best for to turtle soup lower timeframe enter with tight stops and aim for high RR.

Allows to slightly size down, and score big.

Always TP partially at midrange, and leave a runner after taking second partial at range high (the top of CRT candle #️1, as indicated). That way,

"If you're wrong, you still make money, and if you're right, you make a lot of money".

Don't think It will be a wrong  trade here though. Nice clean -FVG located inside the CRT, to trade bearish FVG ICT shorters with stops above CRT high. Nice liquidity to have for second partials.

The data

The data is based on cyclical theory. A type of edge with some sentimental value as it my personal favorite and first real edge in the market when I started trading years ago.

So using cyclical theory and adapting for $BTC, as we know and as I often talk about, $BTC acts in lockstep with the 60 cycle, planting in a low every 60 days in regular pace.

But as with everything in trading, nothing is perfect. The markets are an organic body, there are people involved, and so there is variability to it, and that comes with probability. And managing probability is one of the hardest things in trading, both from a calculation standpoint as from a psychological standpoint (being wrong after taking right actions or being right after taking wrong actions).

So here is how to calculate the chance the low is using cyclical theory.

Firstly, your (my) count has to be correct. But because we have been using this count successfully, netting us wins throughout the entire range of March-Sept, and all the way through to today, firstly (in-live time confirmation check). Secondly, because the last low has been placed during the Trump victory (low was being placed during important, macro events check), it solidifies my count. Finally, black swans should never be a low, so the fact that the Middle East-"WW3" escalation event wick isn't a cycle low, strengthens my count even more. Besides, especially for $BTC (and it's volatility), these counts are hard to get wrong. So yes, I am confident in this count (by all means, try it yourself or use your own)

So using this count, and backtracking it completely all the way to 2015 on one hand, you can simply collect all the lengths of each cycle (again do this yourself if keen).

I did just that, i.e. 52 cycles, the average length is 60.5 days, and the standard deviation is 12.73 days.

So using the same count, we are currently on day 66 (where the last low has been placed).

Making the simple assumption of a normal distribution (cycle lengths are assumed to carry normality), that structures 66.64% of the cycles below 66 days, and 33.36% of the cycles above 66 days.

In other words the chances the low is in on day 66, is 66.4% (make it 67%).

A nice chance, which will only get larger as the days count, using only cycles as an edge.

Tight or Loose, Passive or Aggressive Trading Management? The Key to Winning in Any Trading Scenario

So, with the recent public success of the Astro Block and all calls based on it on my twitter page, but also the overall years long success privately with it, I mentioned how I was going to write a post about "advanced trading management" because to handle the sharpest edge, it often comes with specific and finetuned trading management tactics that go with it. Besides that, your trading management can besides that also depend on the type of edge you have available at a given time for optimal profit (are you more confident in bias or in level-to-level level at the time). 

Most of the guru's on twitter only show you one style (amongst the small selection who show trades at all for starters), either never using a stoploss and just getting liquidated or telling you to "always use a stoploss" as if getting stopped is their favorite thing in the world and as if a price passing a certain level in the price dimension completely invalidates a trade.

It sometimes doesn't, it just puts you in a drawdown you don't like anymore whilst the trade could still be valid (sweeping the low or deviating or even inviting a low timeframe opposite hedge), i.e. you're trading your P&L in essence.

Market makers for instance never use such hard one-level type of stoploss, instead they hunt those exact ones in non obvious ways.

So we know and have proof things aren't as simple as one management style so it's up to you if you want to educate yourself beyond.

On that note, I just wanted to put out the different styles of management that exist alongside the conditions/times you want to use it. Will not only give you more perspective on how you to manage certain edges such as the Astro Block, but it will in general help you use more of your own discoveries and edges more creatively and therefore allow you to extract more money more consistently from the market which we all (should) strive to do constantly.

It will also answer in advance many questions I often get of why I add to positions at certain times, why I exit, why I use an SL in certain cases, and why not in other cases.

Finally, if you have your management locked down, it becomes exponentially harder for your friends to fud you out of your trades as an added bonus because your plan just has that extra dimension personalization.

This is by no means a full guide because that takes a long time and the magic is in the practice. But it all starts with awareness and this post probably will be long enough already on the basics.

Enough ranting let's get to it.

What is an edge

Before discussing the management styles, going over what an edge is and what types is necessary to avoid confusion as everyone sees it differently so just wanted to give a peak of my own library.

What everyone agrees on, is typically and simply said that an edge is a proven advantage based on ideally both market logic (transparent edges) and/or historical data (black box edges) over a significant period of time in the markets. And if used properly (with the right management) it gives you the ability to trade profitably.

Often confused with it is "a strategy" and a full "trading system". As you know, a strategy includes the entry and exits of trades along with an edge and a system includes a confluence of multiple edges and/or strategies into your whole personal boundaries of trading (you typically only have one set system). But to me, a system also includes a confluence of multiple edges both from the black box side as from the transparent side (to have both data and logic backing you), and they are most importantly also required to not have too much correlation within my system with each other. Because yes if RSI goes, then the Mac-D (two indicators I never use but just for illustration) probably goes up too, so adding a bullish Mac-D to your already bullish RSI doesn't really ad confidence, only fake confidence.

Safest is for example to combine different classes of edges to avoid correlation.

Such classes are personal but I classify them as: a magnet edge, i.e. you expect price to pull towards that level before too much movement against it, a momentum edge, i.e. you expect price to continue, a bias edge, i.e. you knowing on a given timeframe if price will generally go up, down, or sideways (yes, there are three biases in trading), a reactionary edge (level edge) i.e. you expect price to if it reaches the level, and a reversal edge (i.e. you predict the trend to reverse and the bias to change.

Some data or logic gives you more than one, for example the FOMC reversal edge is both a reversal edge and a bias edge, because, as you know, it often goes from up to down immediately or vice versa.

But the edge of cyclical timing is only a reversal edge because the cyclical low could be in but the bias could change from down to sideways for the rest of the cycle or from down to back upwards (both cases price reverses but only in the latter you make money on the expected bias change).

Both FOMC reversals as cyclical timing have no levels in their edge included.

Typical level edge is an volume 'n POC visit or a liquidity sweep.

A momentum edge is for example the market putting in a large green candle body candle, sweeping the high on the next candle and retracing quickly close to prior candle (big green candle) low. Momentum is still up but according to OHLC theory, the candles low is unlikely to be taken so you long expecting continued upside momentum.

And the Astro Block is an example of a magnet edge, as the level always (so far) gets tapped, but it's also a momentum edge because it's often tapped in the midst of trend so it continues (if you have time and back test all my posts where I used Astro Blocks in the past, you notice, for the ones following me for a while, remember the October tap and the tap in December 2023, price continued to new weekly and even all time highs).

It is also a bias edge if found with initial momentum against and then combined with basic range theory (a range is set far below a bullish Astro block, a low is swept = expect upside bias towards it, just like this recent one), and it also usually gives a local reaction.

So it is everything except a reversal edge (because it already is a momentum edge, it can't be a reversal edge at the same time).

There are more types of edges, but to keep it short enough, so far a quick overview of some important edges to help you on your way.

Trading management types

So now into trading management types.

There are infinite possibilities, but they can be easily classified and by far my favorite breakdown is using poker as a reference, because poker is almost identical to trading except in trading you are less bound to sizes and edges are more significant and no one is forcing a size upon you so you can allow yourself to make more mistakes. On the flipside, in trading, you are also less susceptible to feeling your mistakes as no outside human influence is impacting or punishing or even taunting you emotionally. Trading is basically poker against fairly predictable AI who rarely (never) go all in.

So from that reference, the 4 styles are: Tight Aggressive (TIP), Tight Aggressive (TAG), Loose Passive (LOP) and Loose Aggressive (LAG).

TAG

Tight and aggressive is probably the most relatable for less patient traders because they take a lot of trades (likely on low timeframe) off of levels and place a tight stoploss, and attempt to score high RR trades and win big on a runner.

This works only when you in fact play tight because hitting high RR's either requires a lot of luck, a very sharp edge and a lot of patience, or, most commonly, multiple attempts. So that only works when you use your ammo slowly.

You also need to be very sharp on your profit taking and knowing when to move your SL up to decrease risk (as TAG players love to do). Otherwise, you end up with large fluctuations in realized drawdown causing revenge trading spirals (which is a general negative of a developing beginner TAG). So you need high focus as you need to constantly gage when price no longer revisits certain levels and you often get taken out earlier than you want.

Frontrunning (always possible) is also very bad for these type of players because a front run takes away multiple losses (they aim for high RR's and/or high size). You often hear excuses of "I'd rather be front run than lose" or "got frontrun but at least I didn't lose money".

But as a TAG, missing winners is easy, missing losers is hard.

"The path towards your SL goes past your entry, the path towards your TP sometimes doesn't".

Another negative is that you can't go too high in size for slippage reasons (on top of larger fees already) so you need liquidity (which is a restriction) and more than you think. Especially on high leverage using tight SL's or illiquid alts.

The major positive though is that it keeps you constantly in tune with the market because you are almost always invested or ready to pull the trigger and if you are good, your equity curve steadily grows and grows fast.

Takes a lot of practice, skill and focus but growth curve is quick.

I would use TAG especially if you are confident in your level game, good at low timeframe order flow both on reaction and follow through, and have a physical setup (like a streamdeck - google it) to quickly get out of trades on limit orders (to limit fees).

I would also try to use your bias edge as much as possible just in case because runners make up a lot of your bread despite them being much harder to catch as a TAG. You don't need to be right all the time because you can make money or break even when your bias is wrong.

TIP

Tight and passive traders are more beginner friendly from the technical side, but to be good, you need to be a rock because you need to sit on your hands for the majority of the time. You basically wait forever to have "all stars align" and then you pull the trigger. And then you need to be confident enough the entire trade to not get ruined or talked out of your trade.

Also consider news events, unexpected events to disrupt your long awaited entry.

Interesting style because you practice patience hard. Works well if your edge is well defined and easy to detect. Also works well if you are starting out and only have one type of edge and have the patience to wait it out and only get involved when it happens. It also keeps you off the charts a lot and allows you to have a life outside of trading.

The skill of mastering reactionary bias (level bias) is important here as well although less important than for TAG, but it does always gives you that boost and ads to your chances of not losing, or opens doors towards more hybrid TIP and TAG.

Finally, it allows more size than TAG, but less than the loose styles.

Downsides are fairly limited but obviously missing trades is detrimental, you also tend to lose touch with the market and are very susceptible to tilt and revenge trading after losses.

Frontrunning is also a big issue here for the same reasons as with TAG.

Finally, market makers love to source, front run and exploit tight passive players and find their stop losses because when their edge gets taken out they are usually stuck for a long time (revenge trade = free money) so your edge needs to be well back tested and include that to outsmart the market makers. They also rarely trade so sizes are larger.

Only recommended for highly patient and very confident traders with a very confident bias and level edge with a high win rate (and often a low frequency).

"Your edge is your patience" to its extreme.

LOP

Loose passive involves having a strong bias, but a careful and slow management.

Often recommended when you have a strong bias but only want to go heavier when you are certain on confirmation.

Next to tight-passive, probably one of my favorite styles because it keeps you very closely involved and positioned into the market yet it makes you feel pain when confirmation isn't here yet. Once confirmation arrives, the trend has already reversed, most of your momentum edges start to engage alongside reversal edges being part of recent history and you gain confidence.

It also works well if you are good at detecting the higher timeframe direction and bias, which is also its downside (you need to be confident in your bias).

Finally, for the developing trader, it makes you resilient to revenge trading because having slow built small positions and partial size already running (yet small size) prevent you having the revenge trade big losses and make you feel like you are winning and not missing out.

I personally don't spend as much time as I used to on perfecting to detect reactions and am left with spending most of my time researching direction and bias and especially in crypto at all times, this works very well as long as you can keep your greed in check.

Astro Blocks and cycle theory also give me a strong and clear-cut bias and along with reactions and confirmation with clear POI's and paired with an obvious counter narrative, it always feels nice to compound higher (or sometimes even lower) on very slowly built positions, to always have that comfortable entry where very passive (sleepy) players suddenly want to rush for a position, pumping your bags (or dumping your shorts). Typically at a time the market pulls back (if it happens) and where you remain comfy whilst the rest is compromised.

This style allows you to not be at the charts too often, and prevents missing any moves (completely avoids front running).

It also offers the ability to play with a lot of size because you truly build your position and take your time

LAG

Loose and aggressive is very versatile and probably the most complex style to master. In poker you are considered very hard to exploit by enemies as a LAG yet the journey is emotional. Same goes to LAG traders' low exploitability by the market makers.

In trading, it means taking aggressive positions at clear points of interest and upon clear theses, sometimes longing or shorting early because you are confident (and don't want to miss out), or taking heavy put hedges on longs because you are bullish but are fairly certain it's too early. 

Or you just want to position heavy in a market with prices that are too cheap for you and are a confident TAG trader so you are always able to position aggressively high timeframe and play hedges low timeframe as long as necessary.

Sometimes you are 4 BTC long and 3 BTC short but you know you are fine because order flow is bullish and you are close to long target so you plan on closing both.

Works well and only well if you are good with numbers, constantly consider your liquidation points and are used to hedging a lot of your trades and are organized/good at keeping overview.

It is also the best at preventing frontrunning and missing moves as you are often aggressively positioned.

There are also times where you really are that confident in a large move up that you are totally fine losing 10% or more of your account being liquidated for the rewards of a home run, but don't want to be wicked or tricked by the market makers to ruin your trade. So you loosen management and increase aggression.

Not often recommended for individual traders, although good to be aware of and mix into hybrids.

This style is mostly used by market makers, who hedge often, use large size and like to confuse retail by "strange" moves in the order flow and books, so far that reason, also good to be aware of this style.

Personal choice and hybrids

I started out as a TIP for years but developed my personal favorite from there towards TAG as I increased skill for low timeframe, although I have been evolving back towards TIP for low timeframe plays but with a slightly wider SL (slight shift towards LAG) and more aggressive entry as well as more aggressive TP's to both prevent frontrunning and losing a trade I have been patient for. It's also natural to be between TAG and TIP because if you have a lot of edges and strategies, you can have multiple TIP style selective entries which turn you into a TAG hybrid with less patience needed, best of both worlds.

In terms of higher timeframe, I used to snipe TIP-style too, but that is sometimes too disengaging so I enjoy LOP the most for the reasons mentioned but sometimes I use LAG if I am very confident in my bias, yet expect a lower timeframe drop, or have a close by magnet below and a larger magnet above.

For example, if there is an Astro Block 5% above, or a very obvious liquidity sweep into a very bearish sentiment, yet the cycle seems early to be finished and there is an untapped POI above a clear low that needs to be run, I still don't want to miss the move at all in case it gets front run or I miss an mmd. So I may go more aggressive on longs early, for example long 2 $BTC, but short the move down lower size as a hedge to complete the move and score + cover longs whilst dca'ing down.

If the short doesn't work, the short is lower size so you close both on the liquidity grab long TP with a lower profit.

Why not just take a lower size? Because you classify your trades respective to their edges and timeframes which is a good practice. You also keep your focus on wins, not losses and it puts your mind at ease, you don't worry about the aggressive long and you can make money on a bigger short than you usually would.

So the overall reward is always bigger.

Conclusion

So here you go, there are many styles. And in short, your tightness and aggression often comes down to personal preference, but can't stress enough how it often doesn't and it's good to be aware of all styles.

Sometimes you are very confident in your bias and have a lot of edge on that available, yet you don't have a clear invalidation formed, or cant afford to be invalidated and miss the second attempt whilst asleep for example). Sometimes that invalidation forms later in the trade, and sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes your edge allows you to be more aggressive as your confidence increases and sometimes you are unsure due to higher timeframe conditions and want/need to be more passive. So you adjust your tightness and aggression accordingly.

Bias edges need loose management, level edges need tight management, reversals take time so they need a more passive style, and sometimes you need to be fast and aggressive when confidence quickly rises.

With only one style, you will miss out more than you win which affects you psychologically and thus you may spiral down or are simply not as good of a trader (or investor).

For all those reasons, you want to be able to handle all basic trading styles and switch between (sometimes during the same trade) as it allows you to make money more often, more consistently and act more consciously and also make it easier to give the edges you find a meaning.

It all looks pretty when you score a clean 20R trade, without the 21 -R's being shown, but in the end, what makes you money?

It's winning more than you lose, and that can be done with every style, more often if you master more.

And more wins and less losses means more confidence, riding the spiral up, not down.

So I would always suggest to consume courses from experts who design them in hands-on ways (very importantly) or straight to-the-point hands on mentorships from people who have experience to accelerate your learning much faster than books.

So for those reasons, I don't really like to recommend books.

For example, I would never read the book "Elliot Wave Principles" by Frost & Prechter", and stay away from theory and implied and illusioned "aha-moments" and rather get into to-the-point and actionable Elliot Wave theory if you want to both save time and set yourself up for rewards. Efficiency is everything.

With all that said, I have read one book, which can be truly helpful IMO.

This book is from D. Kahneman, a Nobel Prize winner, engineer, mathematician, inventor and expert in psychology, a perfect mix of expertise to weaponize yourself optimally for trading, one could without a doubt say

About the content, don't want to spoil too much, but the title saids all. There are times to think fast (and therefore emotionally/intuitively), and times to think slow (and therefore logically, with deep thinking and reasoning). For example, to make the quick and swift dribble in the heat of a high level soccer match and score a goal, you may need to think fast and intuitively and thinking slow-strategically is the worst thing you can do. But in trading, thinking fast and emotionally hurts you.

He explains the differences well and when to use either way of thinking in a number of situations and also ties it together with and goes deep into how people are bad at statistical thinking, and why that is.

So this book doesn't teach you trading itself, but as you read it, you will realize how it teaches you the full mindset of how to think, why and how to remain persistent, so so well, and is the single best book IMO to keep you motivated and on the right track (as well as recognize when you are and when you are not) and not on destructive paths.

I only read a few books and this one was the final one and I decided that that is all I needed years back when I started and I haven't looked back since. I read it again recently and truly enjoyed it.

As you know, I am partnered with Bybit. 

Not in a classic way, as I do not make any money off this, I am doing this to run my fee refund trading program, resend you your commissions and therefore help you become more profitable, whilst at the same time recommending to put your capital on a safe exchange and very utile exchange (disclaimer).

I researched hard into this and given all the bad publicity, and before I head into some negativity myself, I just want to start this post with mentioning with just a few core reasons below why I think Bybit is so good, not mentioned nearly enough. All you hear is "they will be fine".

>Ben (CEO) is transparent, acts normal and doesn't try to take a hostile role.
>1 to 1 backed assets
>Second highest non washed trading volume (after Binance)
>Unified Trading account (use all assets as collateral so you never need to hold any USDT if you don't want to)
>Second biggest support list of altcoins after MEXC
>Supported by CZ, the CEO of binance (amazing because he theoretically is a competitor)
>One of the best coded UI's and system overload handling capabilities (Bybit has the cleanest record of not going down during big crypto crashes)
>Large balance sheet enough to withstand breaches (proven if and after this dust has settled)
>Exchanges with one of the least amount scam wicks (not found any myself on Perp contracts)

These perks are hard to find on other exchanges IMO.

But recently, ironically, that "safe" exchange has been breached with a hack, so I had a round of discussion with the ref traders in the dm's to process some feedback from which this post follows.

So below just a rundown of the situation, my own comments and what I am doing for full disclosure as many veterans have been through (many) similar situations, some are detrimental, some are not, so I fully see how a situation like this can be overwhelming. So form that angle, I hope this post will help you, even if you don't trade on the exchange.

The situation

Very briefly, as it has been addressed everywhere, Bybit has been breached by the hacker group Lazarus, who works for the North Korean government (@ZachXBT sorted this out if I am correct - amazing work).

This resulted in a loss of around $1.5 bn. That sounds a lot, and it is (it's the biggest heist in crypto history).
But Bybit is not your exchange next door, it's one of the richest exchanges in all of crypto, and had at the time of breaching, a total balance sheet of north of $14bn, so at the time of the breach, they had just under 90% of their funds left.

Now I don't know about how they will recover the $1.5 bn, seems like they are actively running bounty programs and receiving support, but unless more than 90% of capital is withdrawn before they can recover the losses, they will be totally fine as all their assets are backed 1 to 1 with on chain proof, hence why Ben (Bybit CEO) tweeted that out.

My thoughts

All in all, a withdrawal of 90%+ that fast seems highly unlikely given the large support of Bybit by people even like CZ himself (CEO of Binance) (for starters) and others.

CZ supports transparency as he always saids, fair (as fair as possible) business and clean sheets. He knows Bybit tries to do things right hence his support (unlike FTX, which he didn't support and against whom he took a rather hostile role, and Mt. Gox) .

He also knows what it's like to be hacked, as Binance in 2019 has also been breached for $50 million at the time.

And regarding the Mt Gox situation, at the time, they lost 650,000 BTC, and had 800,000 BTC, roughly speaking. So they lost 76%. Completely different situation.

Regarding FTX.. Yeah... that is just a result of when you do not back your assets 1 to 1, have one of your main holdings go to near zero ($LUNA), all your assets crash, and thinking you can get away with it even after a bank run. A huge internal problem.

My actions

So, given the situation, at first I was shocked, but after seeing the numbers, there was no need to panic. It gave me a smile after I saw who it was, because Bybit just survived (yes) a massive attack.

I used to have 50% of my assets on Bybit which is arguably too much, I personally now halved that and put some more on the cold wallets (please get one if you don't have one already - NFA). Because I took this hack as another reminder that nothing is safe, so I spread my risk more optimally. The universe is my teacher.

Conclusion

So my advice with situations like this, look at them piece by piece, use common sense, and decide what you do about it.

This is clearly very similar to the Binance hack in 2019, and very different from Mt. Gox and FTX. And Binance is still thriving and stronger than ever.

But this is X, people will do everything they can for engagement and make it look worse or better rather than running over facts. So here my non engagement baited full summarized rundown, + using some common sense along with the actions I took.

The breach was a nice reminder that this is crypto after all, hacks happen all the time (any yield farmers here?), it's all about optimizing how you spread your risk and DYOR on what happens before it does and after.

Are your assets safer in things like metamask or phantom wallet if they are unprotected with a Ledger or Trezor? Don't think so either. On cold wallets? Yes, of course, but makes them harder to access. Balance is key.

With all that said, well done Bybit IMO. Being social engineered is rough and seems like a rookie mistake. But it's the only way hackers operate these days. No one knows exactly how it happened and likely never will. So we can't say if they handled the hack itself well or not.

What we do know is that everything after  the fact is clearly being handled well and damage is limited.

They didn't stop withdrawals, the operations kept going. People who are not on X probably are not even aware of the situation, and their business keeps on running.

So, put some extra coins in cold wallets to be safe, but I think safe to assume they will be just fine.

Current Win streak - Trade review - Where price goes next

Alright so we're on a bit of a hot streak (5 wins) recently, with just over half of the final trade still running.

So just like my occasional review on "an interesting loss" when I get one, I decided to do a quick snapshot review of a particular types of trades happening a lot on this win streak as from wins you can also learn as much as from losses.

And although every trade has been called out live on my twitter timeline (both entry and exit), there is still always that factor of doubt of pulling the trigger and that syndrome has been popping up in the comments (mostly from new people or non-followers who had doubts or opposite stance but now converted and want to learn).

And the way it has been repeating has been forming a pattern so just a quick write-up to address that as a take-away.

Hope it will help, this is is not a hindsight review, because indeed everything has been acted upon live.

Review

So basically, and typically, for $BTC, there are two types of trades. Fast ones (where you need to enter quick, have no or little chance for a retest), and often take profit quickly, and slow ones (type 2), where you need a lot of patience, to ultimately enter.

Type 2 is by nature often countertrend and Type 1 with the trend.

What I often see with type 1 is that indeed, they are missed a lot (but at least people have been helped to wait for lower in that case). On the flip side, type 2 is often taken too early.

So the message I want to give with this review is to really make you think consciously of which type of trade each trade is, and therefore you'll know if you have to act straight away as soon as price hits peak (like the type 1 short on the chart), or be on the other side of the spectrum and wait "that extra day or week".

Most people take the trade somewhere in the middle (too late at type 2, too early for type 1 and get rekt on both). But as we know, our brain is wired to always "mid curve", yet mid curving almost never works, which is exactly why the market counteracts our psychology, nothing new.

Another observation is that the harder the type 1 trade is to catch, the further we are into the reversal zone. Which also was the case with this short on 3. of Feb.

On the flip side, the longer the wait on a type 2 trade, the bigger the reversal will be (chopping longer wears out more players).

Example

So those are the basic principles. And in terms of the recent win streak, the final two trades were exactly a type 1 and 2 trade. With the type 1 trade, a lot of misses have been commented "Oh missed this one" "That was fast, Astro I slept through your tweet, missed it" "Can i short or do I wait for retest?". And on the type 2 trade, a lot of comments on "I am getting chopped up" "When do we long Astro?" "Are you long yet?" "Do I long now?"

In terms of social media and twitter, the type 1 trade barely gets spoken about or called out because it happens quick, maybe only the day traders take it as an intraday trade and end up with a big "runner" (maybe they know, maybe they didn't). Where I just call it out as my bread and butter swing trade and treat it like any other (to keep things simple for your and my spreadsheets)

And the type 2 trade typically involves people calling the low early once, or twice, and then followed by silence/cynicism, on the second low (the actual low, way later, in this case, where the Astro Block was cleared).

Takeaways

So next time you take a (any) trade, especially on $BTC, try to be conscious, is this going to be a fast (type 1) or slow/patient (type 2) trade.

Try to identify if how far in the trend the trade is "How far in the trend are we?". And that's not hard, just ask yourself: is the trend obvious? Then it's probably far in the trend. Is there a lot of chop and stop hunts? Probably reversal and a new trend.

And when we are far in the trend, that doesn't mean you can't take a trend trade just because you think "the trend is obvious so everyone is going to trade the trend, therefore we reverse". Not true, but it does mean, given that we are far in the trend, the entry will be fast and unforgiving so that not many people are able to catch it (almost a "knife catch", just like this recent short at 102 k on the 3rd of Feb). Because then people still short the bottom (enter late) into the chop -> reversal.

On the flip side, if the reversal comes, that is candy land for whales and market makers (they stop hunt a lot and draw out time). So be aware of that, and be on the patient side. Wait longer than normal especially if you have many records in your journal where you entered early.

Those two things will help you a lot both on the trading side of things (on the H1-H6-H12-Daily timeframes) and investing side of things (on the W-M-Q timeframes).

So you hear a lot of experience traders say "trade less frequently, size down, to increase confidence, use only one strategy". That will help, but only answers the type 2 trade of the spectrum.

I personally advocate to be aware of all situations of the market (type 1 and type 2 is a good start) so you always know or have a gage where the market will go and why. That way, you prevent losing touch or becoming lazy, or worse, waiting forever for an entry and missing it because you had real life catch up on you.

Doesn't mean you always have to take a trade for every move you think the market will go, but it does mean you will always be learning.

Master this and you'll be one step closer to not doubting yourself when a trade comes.

Hope this helps.
